title: Short codes and POST /shorten
idea: `POST /shorten` takes a long URL from a logged-in user and returns a short code: seven random characters made by `nanoid(7)`.
points: `requireAuth` runs first, so only a logged-in user reaches the handler.
A Zod schema accepts only `http` and `https` URLs; anything else gets `400`.
`nanoid(7)` picks seven characters from a 64-symbol alphabet of letters, digits, `_` and `-`.
Random codes can collide. The `unique` column added next rejects a repeat.

steps.caption: A logged-in client sends a token and `{ url }`.
Zod checks that `url` is a valid `http` or `https` URL.
The handler calls `nanoid(7)` and has a new short code.
It replies `201` with `{ shortCode }`. Nothing is saved yet.
A second request carries an `ftp:` URL. It passes `requireAuth`.
Zod rejects it, so the route sends `400`. `nanoid` never runs.
A third request has no token and stops at the first check.

code.title: POST /shorten
code.caption: Two new lines do the work: validate, then `nanoid(7)`. Everything below the controller is setup.

walk.text: Only `http` and `https` pass. Plain `z.url()` also accepts `ftp:` and `javascript:`.
A bad body gets `400` with the same `issues` shape as signup.
Make the code. Nothing is stored yet; the next lecture adds the table.
A stand-in for the real middleware: no `Authorization` header means `401`.
No token gives `401`. A bad URL gives `400` and the issue list.
Two valid requests: each code has 7 characters, and the codes differ.

pitfalls: Avoid counters and `Math.random()` for codes: they are predictable. Use `nanoid`.
`z.url()` alone accepts `javascript:` and `ftp:` URLs; restrict the protocol to `http` and `https`.
Call `express.json()` before the route, or `req.body` is `undefined`.

options: Codes are random, so repeats are rare but possible
It checks the database for repeats
Codes count up: a1, a2, a3
quiz.why: `nanoid` only generates random text. It cannot see your table, so uniqueness must come from the database.

takeaway: Validate the URL, generate a random code, and let the database enforce uniqueness.

starters: What happens if nanoid makes the same code twice?
